highlights.text: derives ṭ-r-f from two distinct roots: (1) the edge or border of a thing, and (2) a movement of the eyelids
ṭaraf = the edge/tip of a thing, a garment, or a wall
originally the movement of the eyelids in looking; by extension it also names the eye itself
eyes with a languorous "sickness" in their glance slay their lovers yet do not revive them
Opposite of light.
Putting a thing out of its proper place, wrongfully.
The base word is ظُلْمَة (ẓulma, darkness; plural ظُلُمَات), also called ظَلَام (ẓalām)
The verb ظَلَمَ / يَظْلِمُ / ظُلْم means to wrong.
cited with Kaʿb's line ("...and whoever resembles his father has done no wrong")
highlights.note: proverb with Kaʿb, lived into Islam

highlights.text: illustrated by Zuhayr's line about a generous man "sometimes wronged, so he bears it" (fa-yaẓẓalimu)
treats b-q-y as a single root meaning permanence / enduring (al-dawām)
baqiyya / buqyā = sparing, clemency, mercy shown to someone
Shāhid from al-Nābigha: you will not "keep" a brother you never reproach for a fault, since no man is entirely faultless.
The ḥadīth of Muʿādh «بَقَيْنَا رسولَ الله» ("we waited for the Messenger of God") uses this "waiting" sense.
treats B–W–L as two separate roots: (1) fluid that seeps or flows out; (2) al-rūʿ — the inner part of a person into which a thought falls
مَا خَطَرَ بِبَالِي, "it never crossed my bāl," glossed as "it was not cast into my rūʿ (inward self)."
a wineskin that bursts and gushes its drink; attested in ʿAdī's poetry
Ibn Muqbil's verse uses the phrase for the mirage of the Ḥimyarī uplands
He cites Ibn ʿAbbās, asked about performing wuḍūʾ with milk: "I do not mind it in the least; be easy and you will be dealt with easily."
one core idea: to incline or draw something toward yourself by means of a sound or speech that you produce
The base verb is دَعَا / يَدْعُو / دُعَاء (to call).
Shāhid: a line of Imruʾ al-Qays ("...the people do not claim that I flee")
doubled d-r points to two root meanings: one thing issuing from another, and agitation (unsteady movement) in a thing
darra is the pouring of clouds, and clouds of abundant rain are midrār
the piercing, shining star, likened to durr and named after it for its whiteness
al-Hudhalī's verse on a pearl over which "the sweet water lingers and surges"
going ahead in order to guide.
sending a kindness.
هَدَيْتُهُ الطَّرِيقَ ("I guided him on the road") = I went ahead to direct him
الْهُدَى (right guidance) as the opposite of الضَّلَالَة (going astray)
الْهَدِيَّة (a gift) = a kindness sent to someone one loves
A verse of poetry illustrates a spear-point as a man's "guide" through the land.
resting on two root meanings: cutting, and the drawing-together of a thing
al-jubb is a well.
Abū Khirāsh, describing an eagle that lifts its prey and then lets it drop, says the prey "struck the hard ground (al-jabūb) with the place between its eyes"
the root has one core meaning: cutting (al-qaṭʿ)
arḍ juruz is land with no vegetation, as if growth had been cut off from it
Ash-Shammākh's line is cited describing a rasp in the nasal passage and nostrils.
"A hating woman will not be satisfied except with a jarzah"
one core meaning: turning/rotation, and by extension, gathering into a mass
as though the sun were entirely gathered/bundled up
He wraps/turns the one over the other and the other over the one
means to turn away and swerve off from God's dīn
المُلْتَحَد (al-multaḥad) means a refuge or shelter
A line of Ḥumayd ibn Thawr: "Enough for me of supporting the two Khubaybs, enough / the leader is not the miserly, deviating one (al-mulḥid)."
highlights.note: Ḥumayd ibn Thawr, lived into Islam

highlights.text: Two distinct sound roots: (1) the settling of a liquid in its resting-place, and (2) a kind of sound/outcry.
The proverb "huwa sharrābun bi-anquʿ" — "he is a drinker at [hidden] pools" — describes someone who repeats a matter over and over
naqaʿa al-ṣawt — a sound rose up, illustrated with a line of poetry about a war-cry gathering people for battle
this root carries two core meanings: (1) aiming/purposing toward something, and (2) the stone/pit of something
al-nawā meaning "the pit of a date."
analyzes ق ن ع as containing two distinct core ideas, plus a possible third
al-qāniʿ being "the one who begs," so called because he turns toward the person he's asking
iqnāʿ meaning "raising something up with no downward dip."
A supporting verse contrasts a man's well-managed wealth, which spares him need, as more honorable than begging (qunūʿ)
which the exegetes explained as "raising their heads."
a single core sense: one thing rising or mounting upon another
رَكِبَ (rakiba, "he rode/mounted")
الرِّكَاب (al-rikāb): riding-camels
الرَّكْب (al-rakb) and الْأُرْكُوب (al-urkūb): a riding party
one root whose single underlying idea is bewilderment or disorientation (ḥayra)
سُكْر (sukr) is the drunkenness produced by drink
{إِنَّمَا سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا} — "our eyes have merely been sukkirat", i.e. dazed
سَكَر (sakar, with two a-vowels) is simply "drink" (al-sharāb)
Shāhid: a line of Aws — "My nights are made yet longer in their length; they are neither mild (ṭalq) nor still (sākira)."
سريع = "swift": "he came swiftly"; "a swift horse," plural "swift horses" (سراع)
يسارعون / يتسارعون = "they vie and race toward the good"
Proverb: "How are the slow to overtake the swift, the short-paced the wide-striding?"
a verse by Mālik b. Zaghba al-Bāhilī on aversion arriving "so soon" while the bond of union frays
وهب (wahaba) — to give something as a gift
al-Wahhāb "the abundant in gifts."
Al-wasan and al-sinah (this author treats سِنَة as belonging to the same root) both name a light doze or drowsiness that overtakes a person
a verse by Ḥumayd ibn Thawr in which a rain-cloud "visits" a meadow the way a night-phantom visits a sleeper
highlights.note: Ḥumayd ibn Thawr, lived into Islam

highlights.text: the three letters kh-y-m form a single root meaning "to stay/reside" and "firmness, steadfastness."
al-khaymah ("tent") — well known; explicitly named for the fact that one resides (aqāma) in/at it
Supported by a line of poetry describing "a stacked frame of tent-poles" left standing [of an abandoned camp]
